Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Learning Objectives — Deep Dive

screens.title: Understanding systemd service states
screens.narratorSegment: A clear mental model of systemd service states speeds diagnosis. 'Active (running)' means systemd has a live service process; 'inactive (dead)' means the unit is not running and was not recently active; 'failed' indicates an attempted start or runtime error that systemd recorded. The action you take differs by state: if active, you verify the service performs its function; if inactive, you attempt a start and then immediately check journal entries for startup errors; if failed, you should treat the failure as a signal to gather logs rather than restarting blindly. A concrete example: after editing an Apache configuration, systemctl status httpd may show Active: failed with a brief snippet pointing to an ExecStart error; that snippet plus journalctl -u httpd -xe will usually show a configuration syntax error or a missing module. A common misconception is that repeatedly restarting a failed service will resolve the root cause; in reality it can mask intermittent failures and flood logs. Your takeaway: always capture the status output and then run journalctl with unit filtering to read explanatory entries before changing configuration or restarting. What exact journal entries would you save to reproduce the failure on another host?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Understanding systemd service states
Definition
What the common systemd states represent and their diagnostic implication
  • Active (running): service process running; verify functionality and logs for recent errors.
  • Inactive (dead): not running; attempt start and gather startup logs if it fails.
  • Failed: recorded error; inspect journalctl -u <service> -xe for explanatory messages.
Key Takeaway

Capture the status and the associated journal entries before changing configuration or restarting the service.

Concrete example: httpd
# Inspect service status
systemctl status httpd

# If failed, get detailed journal output
journalctl -u httpd -xe
Common mistake: Restarting repeatedly without reading the journal can obscure the original error. Instead, copy the journal excerpt and attach it to your incident notes.

screens.title: Using journalctl to diagnose failures
screens.narratorSegment: Journalctl is the single most useful tool for service-level diagnosis on systemd systems because it aggregates systemd unit logs with timestamps and explanatory text. Start with journalctl -u service -xe to show the unit's recent entries with extended explanation and begin at the end of the log. Use --since and --until to limit the time window when you suspect a change triggered a failure. For live reproduction, run journalctl -f -u service to follow new entries as you exercise the service. A practical example: you run a configuration change, attempt to start the service, and immediately run journalctl -u httpd -xe; you will often see a syntax error or inability to bind a port. A common misconception is that application logs alone suffice; while they are essential, journalctl captures startup failures and system-level messages that apps may not write. When you capture output for an incident report, include the unit-filtered journal and the exact timestamp lines that show the failure, so the event can be correlated to deployments or system changes. Which journal lines would you save to attach to a ticket?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Using journalctl to diagnose failures
Command callouts
# Show recent entries with explanations and jump to the end
journalctl -u httpd -xe

# Follow new journal entries in real time for the unit
journalctl -f -u httpd

# Limit by time window
journalctl -u httpd --since "2026-01-01 10:00:00" --until "2026-01-01 10:15:00"
Use these filters to extract only the relevant lines and include them in your incident notes for reproducibility.
Explanation and example
  • journalctl aggregates systemd and kernel messages that might explain why a service failed before the app could write logs.
  • Follow mode helps when reproducing a failure during a configuration change or a client request.
  • Always note exact timestamps and the first error line; those are the best clues for root cause analysis.
Common Mistake
Relying only on tailing application logs without checking the journal misses system-level failures like missing library loads or unit-level ExecStart errors.

screens.title: Application logs: where to look and how to parse them
screens.narratorSegment: Application logs are often the decisive source for why an application behaves badly. On Red Hat systems many services write to /var/log/ /, for example Apache writes to /var/log/httpd/ and MariaDB to /var/log/mariadb/ or similar locations. Start by locating the error_log and access_log files, then use tail -n and tail -f to see recent entries and live updates. Filter with grep for keywords like error, fail, warning, exception or specific error codes your application produces. Combine grep with awk or cut to show only timestamps and levels if the logs are verbose. A concrete example: while diagnosing a blank page in a web app, tail -f /var/log/httpd/error_log reveals a file permission denied entry with a timestamp that matches a client attempt; this points you to file ownership or SELinux context issues. A common misconception is to assume timestamps are local system time; always ensure you compare timestamps between logs and systemctl journal entries to correlate events. Your practical habit should be: identify the log file, follow the last lines while reproducing the issue, and save the exact log snippet that contains the first error line for later analysis.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Application logs: where to look and how to parse them
Common locations
  • /var/log/httpd/ — Apache access_log and error_log
  • /var/log/mariadb/ or /var/log/mysql/ — database server logs
  • Application-specific directories under /var/log or within app install path
Useful commands
# Follow errors live
tail -f /var/log/httpd/error_log

# Get last 100 lines
tail -n 100 /var/log/httpd/error_log

# Filter for errors
grep -iE "error|fail|exception" /var/log/httpd/error_log
Example scenario
While reproducing a blank page, you run tail -f on the Apache error_log and see a permission denied entry with matching timestamp. That shows the server process couldn't read a file. Next steps include ls -l to check ownership and ls -Zd to check SELinux context.
Pro Tip
Use grep with a time range or use awk to extract timestamps so you can correlate application logs with journalctl entries and firewall events.

screens.title: Troubleshooting web servers vs databases
screens.narratorSegment: Web servers and databases require different targeted checks even though both benefit from the same evidence-first approach. For web servers such as Apache or Nginx, syntax checks on configuration are the first step: apachectl configtest or nginx -t will detect syntax errors that prevent startup. Then verify that the server is listening on the expected ports with ss -tunap and check that the document root exists with appropriate read permissions. If a 'Forbidden' error appears, check SELinux denials in audit. log and verify file contexts with ls -Zd. For databases like MariaDB or PostgreSQL, start with service status and database log files for startup errors, then test client connectivity from the application server with the command-line client and verify the application user has the necessary privileges. A common misconception is treating these two classes the same; for example, restarting a web server often hides a persistent configuration error, whereas a database failure may be caused by corrupted data files or permission issues that require deeper recovery. In practice, keep a checklist for each service type and correlate timestamps between service journals, application logs, and firewall checks to find the single event that started the failure chain.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Troubleshooting web servers vs databases
Web server checklist (Apache/Nginx)
  • Run apachectl configtest or nginx -t to catch syntax errors.
  • Confirm listening ports: ss -tunap | grep :80
  • Verify document root exists and is readable by the server user.
  • Check SELinux context and audit.log for AVC denials.
Concrete command
apachectl configtest
ss -tunap | grep :80
ls -l /var/www/html
ls -Zd /var/www/html
Database checklist (MariaDB/PostgreSQL)
  • Check service status and server logs for startup errors.
  • Test client connectivity from the app host to isolate network vs credentials.
  • Validate database user privileges for the application account.
Concrete command
systemctl status mariadb
# Example client test
mysql -u appuser -p -h 127.0.0.1

screens.title: SELinux and firewall: frequent causes of inaccessibility
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux and firewalld are two security layers that frequently cause services to be inaccessible remotely even when they work locally. Firewalld controls network-level access; use firewall-cmd --list-all to inspect zone rules and verify http and https services are allowed in the public zone. If the port is not open, the server will reject remote connections even if the service listens locally. SELinux enforces mandatory access controls and can prevent a service process from reading files or binding to ports if contexts are incorrect. A common diagnostic step for SELinux is to check /var/log/audit/audit. log for AVC denials or to run ls -Zd on the document root to inspect its SELinux context. Temporarily setting setenforce 0 puts SELinux into permissive mode and can help determine if SELinux is blocking access, but this should only be used for diagnosis and not as a fix. Instead, use semanage fcontext and restorecon to set the correct context. A common misconception is to disable SELinux permanently; prefer applying correct file contexts to maintain security while restoring functionality. SELinux and firewall: frequent causes of inaccessibility means check both firewalld rules and selinux contexts; use permissive mode only for diagnosis and fix contexts with semanage/restorecon.. In practical terms, why a service can work locally but be unreachable remotely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › SELinux and firewall: frequent causes of inaccessibility
Firewalld checks
# Inspect public zone rules
firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=public

# Ensure http and https services are allowed
# or check open ports
ss -tunap | grep :80
If http/https are missing from allowed services, add them with firewall-cmd --add-service= http --permanent and reload. Always verify after reload.
SELinux checks
  • Check file context: ls -Zd /var/www/html
  • Review AVC denials: /var/log/audit/audit.log for messages labeled avc
  • Temporary test: setenforce 0 to see if access is restored (diagnostic only)
Common Pitfall
Don't leave SELinux disabled. Use semanage fcontext and restorecon to set correct contexts as a permanent fix.

screens.title: A reproducible troubleshooting sequence
screens.narratorSegment: Adopting a repeatable sequence reduces time-to-fix and prevents common mistakes. Begin by capturing the service status with systemctl and copy the output into your notes. Next, run journalctl -u service -xe and save the timestamped excerpt that includes the first error. Then locate and follow the application error log with tail -f as you reproduce the failure. After log inspection, verify configuration syntax: run apachectl configtest or nginx -t before any restart. Check that the service listens on the intended port with ss -tunap and review firewalld rules. Inspect SELinux contexts with ls -Zd and audit logs for AVC denials. If all checks point to a configuration or context issue, apply the minimal corrective action and re-check logs rather than applying repeated restarts. Finally, collect artifacts — saved journal excerpts, filtered log snippets, and validation commands — and, where appropriate, automate the checks with Ansible so the same sequence runs across hosts. A common trap is to skip evidence collection and then lose the ability to correlate failures across hosts; always capture the first fail lines and timestamps. A reproducible troubleshooting sequence means capture status and journal, inspect application logs, test syntax, verify ports and security contexts, save artifacts, and automate checks when repeatable.. In practical terms, evidence-first steps to diagnose a failing service. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › A reproducible troubleshooting sequence
Step-by-step cards
  1. Run systemctl status <service> and save the output.
  2. Run journalctl -u <service> -xe and copy timestamped errors.
  3. Follow application logs with tail -f while reproducing.
  4. Test configuration syntax (apachectl configtest or nginx -t).
  5. Verify ports and firewall, then SELinux context if needed.
Example artifact
Save a small incident bundle that includes the systemctl output, a 50-100 line journal excerpt, the last 100 lines of the application error_log, and the output of ls -Zd for the document root. These files let another engineer reproduce your findings.
Key Takeaway
Evidence-first workflows reduce guesswork and enable better collaboration across teams.

screens.title: Automating checks with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible lets you turn your manual troubleshooting sequence into reproducible automation. A small playbook can query systemd status, fetch application logs, and run diagnostic commands like firewall-cmd and ls -Zd on many hosts in one run. The provided playbook demonstrates this pattern: it uses the systemd module to get the httpd service status, conditionally fetches the error_log when a failure is detected, runs firewall and SELinux context checks with command tasks, and reports findings via debug. This combination gives you a consistent incident snapshot from each host so you can compare across an inventory. A common pitfall is running remediation automatically without human review; use playbooks to gather evidence and optionally to perform guarded remediation steps that require explicit approval. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Automating checks with Ansible
Playbook pattern
Register results from systemd checks, use when to fetch logs only on failure, run firewall and SELinux commands, and aggregate artifacts to the control node.
- name: Troubleshoot web service
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Check httpd service status
      systemd:
        name: httpd
      register: httpd_status

    - name: Fetch httpd error log if service is failed
      fetch:
        src: /var/log/httpd/error_log
        dest: /tmp/ansible_logs/{{ inventory_hostname }}/
        flat: yes
      when: httpd_status.status.ActiveState == 'failed'
Practical notes
  • Use changed_when: false for read-only checks to avoid false positives in reports.
  • Delegate aggregation tasks to the control node for central storage of log snippets.
  • Avoid automatic restarts unless the cause is well understood and monitored.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Playbook walkthrough: troubleshoot_app_service.yml
Starter playbook (excerpt)
- name: Troubleshoot Web Application Service
  hosts: appservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Check httpd service status
      systemd:
        name: httpd
      register: httpd_status

    - name: Fetch httpd error log
      ansible.builtin.shell: tail -n 100 /var/log/httpd/error_log
      register: error_log_content
      changed_when: false
      ignore_errors: true

    - name: Save httpd error log to control node
      delegate_to: localhost
      copy:
        content: |
          Error Log from {{ inventory_hostname }}:
          -------------------------------------
          {{ error_log_content.stdout | default('Error log not found or empty.') }}
        dest: "./app_logs/{{ inventory_hostname }}_error_log.txt"
      when: error_log_content.stdout is defined
Why this pattern works
  • Registering outputs allows conditional actions and selective fetching of logs only when useful.
  • Delegating copy tasks to the control node centralizes artifacts for team review.
  • Using changed_when: false keeps the playbook safe to run in production when only collecting data.

screens.narratorSegment: In this hands-on scenario a deployed web app intermittently shows '403 Forbidden' or a blank page. The first step is to reproduce the error while you follow the server logs. A common mistake is to change permissions or disable SELinux without validating the root cause; always collect logs first so your remediation is targeted and reversible. After you gather artifacts, decide whether to update file context with semanage fcontext and restorecon, fix ownership, or correct configuration syntax, then re-test.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will learn a practical, evidence-driven approach to diagnosing services on Red Hat systems. You will become fluent with systemd status checks, service journals, and application log analysis so you can identify configuration errors, permission denials, or port conflicts quickly. We will examine common checks for web servers and databases, show where SELinux and firewalld commonly intervene, and demonstrate how to automate routine checks with Ansible. For example, you will see how a syntax error in an Apache configuration results in a failed service state, and how journalctl plus an application error_log gives the precise line to fix. You will also learn a safe pattern: gather the evidence first, test configuration syntax, then apply fixes; avoid repeated blind restarts which can hide root causes. By the end of this lesson you will know what commands to run, what files to inspect, and how to combine those steps into an Ansible playbook that scales across hosts. Keep a focus on timestamps and specific error keywords when you read logs; they are the clues that lead to a reliable fix.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to diagnose and resolve common issues with systemd-managed services, analyze application logs to find root causes, troubleshoot web and database services, and automate checks using Ansible. First, you'll learn the meaning of service states and how to interpret the output from systemctl and journalctl. Then you'll practice reading application-specific log files and using simple shell tools to filter and follow logs in real time. You will also learn the targeted checks for web servers and databases — configuration syntax tests, port listening verification, document root and permission checks, and database connectivity tests. Finally, you'll see how SELinux and firewalld commonly interfere and how Ansible can gather the same evidence consistently across multiple hosts. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can measure competency: running status checks, extracting relevant log snippets, and producing a small Ansible report that confirms service state and security context. This set of skills will make your troubleshooting efficient and repeatable.

This second objectives slide expands how you will practice each skill and why those checks matter. For systemd status, practice by observing a failing service and reading the included journal excerpt; that shows you the precise failure mode instead of guessing. For application logs, practice filtering for error, fail, exception and using timestamps to link a code deploy, restart, or client request to observed errors. For web and database troubleshooting, practice the targeted commands: apachectl configtest or nginx -t to find syntax errors, using a client to connect to the database to confirm credentials and network connectivity, and verifying file permissions and SELinux contexts for document roots. For automation, practice writing a small Ansible playbook that queries service states, fetches logs, and reports SELinux contexts to a control node. Each verification milestone should produce an artifact: a service status report, a saved error log snippet, or a playbook run that collects evidence from a set of hosts. These artifacts prove your troubleshooting is repeatable and scalable.

A clear mental model of systemd service states speeds diagnosis. 'Active (running)' means systemd has a live service process; 'inactive (dead)' means the unit is not running and was not recently active; 'failed' indicates an attempted start or runtime error that systemd recorded. The action you take differs by state: if active, you verify the service performs its function; if inactive, you attempt a start and then immediately check journal entries for startup errors; if failed, you should treat the failure as a signal to gather logs rather than restarting blindly. A concrete example: after editing an Apache configuration, systemctl status httpd may show Active: failed with a brief snippet pointing to an ExecStart error; that snippet plus journalctl -u httpd -xe will usually show a configuration syntax error or a missing module. A common misconception is that repeatedly restarting a failed service will resolve the root cause; in reality it can mask intermittent failures and flood logs. Your takeaway: always capture the status output and then run journalctl with unit filtering to read explanatory entries before changing configuration or restarting. What exact journal entries would you save to reproduce the failure on another host?

Journalctl is the single most useful tool for service-level diagnosis on systemd systems because it aggregates systemd unit logs with timestamps and explanatory text. Start with journalctl -u service -xe to show the unit's recent entries with extended explanation and begin at the end of the log. Use --since and --until to limit the time window when you suspect a change triggered a failure. For live reproduction, run journalctl -f -u service to follow new entries as you exercise the service. A practical example: you run a configuration change, attempt to start the service, and immediately run journalctl -u httpd -xe; you will often see a syntax error or inability to bind a port. A common misconception is that application logs alone suffice; while they are essential, journalctl captures startup failures and system-level messages that apps may not write. When you capture output for an incident report, include the unit-filtered journal and the exact timestamp lines that show the failure, so the event can be correlated to deployments or system changes. Which journal lines would you save to attach to a ticket?

Application logs are often the decisive source for why an application behaves badly. On Red Hat systems many services write to /var/log/ /, for example Apache writes to /var/log/httpd/ and MariaDB to /var/log/mariadb/ or similar locations. Start by locating the error_log and access_log files, then use tail -n and tail -f to see recent entries and live updates. Filter with grep for keywords like error, fail, warning, exception or specific error codes your application produces. Combine grep with awk or cut to show only timestamps and levels if the logs are verbose. A concrete example: while diagnosing a blank page in a web app, tail -f /var/log/httpd/error_log reveals a file permission denied entry with a timestamp that matches a client attempt; this points you to file ownership or SELinux context issues. A common misconception is to assume timestamps are local system time; always ensure you compare timestamps between logs and systemctl journal entries to correlate events. Your practical habit should be: identify the log file, follow the last lines while reproducing the issue, and save the exact log snippet that contains the first error line for later analysis.

Web servers and databases require different targeted checks even though both benefit from the same evidence-first approach. For web servers such as Apache or Nginx, syntax checks on configuration are the first step: apachectl configtest or nginx -t will detect syntax errors that prevent startup. Then verify that the server is listening on the expected ports with ss -tunap and check that the document root exists with appropriate read permissions. If a 'Forbidden' error appears, check SELinux denials in audit. log and verify file contexts with ls -Zd. For databases like MariaDB or PostgreSQL, start with service status and database log files for startup errors, then test client connectivity from the application server with the command-line client and verify the application user has the necessary privileges. A common misconception is treating these two classes the same; for example, restarting a web server often hides a persistent configuration error, whereas a database failure may be caused by corrupted data files or permission issues that require deeper recovery. In practice, keep a checklist for each service type and correlate timestamps between service journals, application logs, and firewall checks to find the single event that started the failure chain.

SELinux and firewalld are two security layers that frequently cause services to be inaccessible remotely even when they work locally. Firewalld controls network-level access; use firewall-cmd --list-all to inspect zone rules and verify http and https services are allowed in the public zone. If the port is not open, the server will reject remote connections even if the service listens locally. Instead, use semanage fcontext and restorecon to set the correct context. A common misconception is to disable SELinux permanently; prefer applying correct file contexts to maintain security while restoring functionality. Keep three core ideas in mind as you troubleshoot services. First, systemctl status combined with journalctl -u is the most direct path to understanding why a systemd-managed service failed. Second, application logs are critical; locate error_log files, use tail and grep to follow and filter, and always save the first error lines with timestamps for reproducible evidence. Third, security layers often cause accessibility problems — check firewalld rules and SELinux contexts before assuming the application itself is broken.
